analysis.one_liner: Lets the Postal Service offer low-cost checking, savings, and small-dollar loans.
analysis.headline: Introduced with two cosponsors, the bill was referred to a Senate committee the day it was filed and died there without a hearing or a vote.
analysis.plain_summary: The Postal Banking Act would have let the U.S. Postal Service offer basic banking directly to the public: small loans up to $500 (up to $1,000 within a year of the first loan), checking and savings accounts up to $20,000, debit cards, check cashing, bill pay, and domestic and international money transfers. The Postal Service would set the rates itself, with loan interest and fees capped near the one-month Treasury rate, and the Federal Reserve would transfer whatever money was needed to run the program. The bill was referred to the Senate Homeland Security and Governmental Affairs Committee and never received a hearing or vote before the Congress ended.
analysis.who_benefits: Roughly the tens of millions of American households that lack bank accounts or rely on costly alternatives: payday borrowers who would get small loans at a fraction of payday-loan cost, people who cash checks at storefronts that take a cut, immigrants and families sending money abroad who pay remittance fees, and people in rural or low-income areas where post offices remain but bank branches have closed. Savings account holders would get an interest-rate floor tied to the FDIC national average.

how_it_helps.text: Would let the Postal Service make small loans of up to $500 at a time (up to $1,000 within a year of the first loan) with total interest and fees capped at 101% of the one-month Treasury rate — a small fraction of what payday lenders typically charge.

Would offer small checking accounts and interest-bearing savings accounts of up to $20,000 per account, with savings rates required to be at least 100% of the FDIC weekly national rate on non-jumbo savings accounts.

Would add check cashing, debit cards, bill pay, online and mobile banking, and money transfers at post offices — services that matter most where bank branches have closed but post offices still operate.

Would require the Federal Reserve to transfer funds sufficient to substantially reduce the number of people who are unbanked or rely on payday loans, check cashing, prepaid cards, and overdraft fees, with annual GAO reports on who uses the products.

analysis.who_pays: Payday lenders, check-cashing outlets, and money-transfer companies would lose customers to a far cheaper public option, and banks would lose fee income from overdrafts and account maintenance. The Federal Reserve would bear the program's funding cost through required transfers, meaning the public balance sheet ultimately backs the loans and accounts; if the Postal Service's loan losses ran high, that cost would land on the public.

drawbacks.text: The funding is open-ended: the bill requires the Federal Reserve to transfer 'such sums as may be necessary,' with no dollar cap, so taxpayers backstop the program through the Fed if loan losses or operating costs exceed revenue.

Capping small loans at roughly the one-month Treasury rate — near zero at the time — leaves the Postal Service no margin to absorb defaults on unsecured loans to borrowers with no credit history, a design an honest supporter would acknowledge is financially risky.

The bill bars the Postal Service from partnering with private banks or contracting with insured depository institutions, so the agency — which was already losing money — would have to build and run a nationwide banking operation on its own.
Caps of $500 per loan and $20,000 per account limit how much the program can do; larger savings balances and bigger credit needs would still have to go to conventional banks or be unmet.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For the households the bill targets, the benefits are concrete and immediate: a $500 loan at a rate near zero instead of a payday loan rolled over at triple-digit annual rates, and check cashing at cost instead of a percentage fee. The costs are real but speculative — an open-ended Federal Reserve funding commitment and default risk the Postal Service has never managed at scale, made riskier by the ban on bank partnerships. A more cautious design might have capped the Fed's exposure or allowed partnerships; this bill chose maximum reach over financial caution. On balance, the upside for unbanked and payday-borrowing households was large, and the downside was a funding risk the bill left unquantified.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the Senate Homeland Security and Governmental Affairs Committee the day it was introduced and died there when the Congress ended, without a hearing, a markup, or a vote.

narrative.text: Senator Kirsten Gillibrand introduced the Postal Banking Act on September 17, 2020, with Senator Bernie Sanders joining as the bill's only other original backer.
The Senate read the bill twice and referred it to the Homeland Security and Governmental Affairs Committee, which was its last action; the committee never held a hearing or advanced it.
The bill ended the 116th Congress in January 2021 with two cosponsors — one Democrat and one Independent — and no vote in either chamber.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Payday lenders, check-cashing outlets, money-transfer companies, and banks that earn overdraft and account fees kept their customers and fee revenue untouched, and the Federal Reserve avoided an open-ended funding obligation. Postal customers gained nothing, because the program never started.

for.name: Kirsten Gillibrand
for.what_they_did: Sponsored and introduced the Postal Banking Act.

for.name: Bernie Sanders
for.what_they_did: Joined the bill at introduction as an original cosponsor.

against.name: Ron Johnson
against.role: Chair, Senate Homeland Security and Governmental Affairs Committee
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled the bill for a hearing or committee vote after its referral; it received no action for the rest of the Congress.

against.name: Mitch McConnell
against.what_they_did: Never brought the bill to the Senate floor at any point in the 116th Congress.

against.name: Payday lenders and check-cashing companies
against.what_they_did: A postal lending program with rates capped near the Treasury rate would directly undercut their core business; the industry has consistently opposed postal banking proposals.

sides.party_line_note: All of the bill's support came from the Democratic side — one Democratic sponsor, one Democratic cosponsor, and one Independent — with no Republican cosponsors and no vote ever taken to test the chamber.

industries.note: The bill would let the Postal Service lend up to $500 at total interest and fees capped at 101% of the one-month Treasury rate, far below the triple-digit annual rates payday loans typically carry. A public option at that price would take away their core product.

industries.industry: Check cashing and money transfer services
industries.note: Post offices would cash checks and send domestic and international remittances directly, competing with storefront check cashers and wire-transfer companies that charge a percentage or flat fee per transaction.

Banks would lose overdraft and account-fee revenue if customers moved to free postal accounts, and the bill specifically bars the Postal Service from partnering with or contracting through insured depository institutions — cutting banks out of the program entirely rather than routing it through them.

The bill hands USPS a new fee-earning line of business funded by Federal Reserve transfers, adding revenue to an agency facing chronic deficits while expanding services at existing post offices. Its gain runs alongside the public's, though it also inherits the default risk on small loans.
